name: Bryggen Hanseatic Wharf
label: Bryggen
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/32669193: the OpenStreetMap point 'Bryggen Hanseatic Wharf'.
notes: The colourful wooden Hanseatic warehouses are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the best-known view of Bergen.

text.description:
Bryggen is the row of old wooden merchant buildings along the eastern side of the Vågen harbour in Bergen. Its name means 'the dock'. It is also called Tyskebryggen, 'the German dock'. Around 1350 a Kontor of the Hanseatic League was established here. Bergen itself is said to have been founded within this area around 1070, and the wharf has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1979.

The buildings you see today are much younger than the site. Fire has swept through Bergen many times, and after a big fire in 1702 the wharf was rebuilt. Another fire in 1955 cleared part of it, and the dig that followed turned up the runic notes known as the Bryggen inscriptions. Today the buildings hold museums, shops, restaurants and pubs.

It photographs well because the narrow, tightly packed gabled fronts make a strong repeating pattern, and the harbour in front gives you open space to step back. Start with a wide view of the whole row, then move closer for details such as gable tops, doors and window shutters. Look for neighbours' roofs and lines of buildings that lead the eye along the front. Keep your phone steady against the pull of the crowd, and check people's heads aren't cutting into your frame.
text.geographic_location: Bryggen runs along the eastern side of the Vågen harbour in Bergen, Norway.
text.directions_text: Head for the Vågen harbour in Bergen; the wharf lines the eastern side of the harbour. From there the wharf is 32 m to the north, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the row of fronts as the eye sees them. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit the whole line in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for gables, signs and window details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From there the long line of gabled buildings sits in front of you with the harbour beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the vertical edges of the buildings up with them so they do not lean. Put the row on a diagonal through the frame to add depth, with a bit of harbour or sky for breathing space. Then take a second shot with the telephoto and fill the frame with just three or four gables. Keep your phone level; if you tilt it upward the buildings will look as if they are falling backwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest building front to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is washing out. Try a Live Photo if boats or people are moving, then pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to evening usually gives warmer light on the fronts. Early morning is typically quieter, if you want fewer people in the picture.

text.access_note: Bryggen is a working part of the city with shops, restaurants and museums, so check the official site before you go for entry to any museum or building.
claims_not_in_sources: The wharf fronts face west across the harbour, so late-afternoon and evening sun is likely to light them.
Early morning is usually quieter than the middle of the day.
Walking along the outside of the wharf buildings and taking photographs there is generally free, while museum entry may need a ticket.
Tilting a phone upward makes tall buildings look as if they lean backwards.

name: Fløibanen Funicular
label: Fløibanen Funicular
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fjellveien' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Fjellveien nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/165297871: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fløibanen, nedre stasjon;Fløibanen' (16 m across).
notes: The funicular runs from the city centre up to Mount Fløyen.

text.description:
Fløibanen is the funicular that carries visitors from the centre of Bergen up the mountain of Fløyen. It is one of Norway's most visited attractions and carries nearly two million passengers a year. The line is 848 m long and climbs 302 m. It is a single track with a passing loop in the middle, so the two cars meet halfway. They are named Blåmann (blue) and Rødhette (red), and together with the white lower station building they echo the colours of the Norwegian flag. The line opened on 15 January 1918.

For a photo, the railway itself is the best subject. Ride to the Fjellveien stop and walk a little back uphill. The frame works because of the two bold colours against the hillside, and because the cars keep coming. Daytime departures run roughly every quarter of an hour, so you can wait for the next pair if you miss one.

If you would rather photograph the white lower station building, Fisketorget gives a view of it from the harbour side. Both spots are only thinly documented, so check the position on the map before you rely on it. Keep your distance from the track and stay on the public path.
text.geographic_location: Fløibanen starts in the centre of Bergen and climbs the hillside towards the mountain of Fløyen.
text.directions_text: Start in the centre of Bergen, where the lower station of the Fløibanen stands. From there the lower station lies to the west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the cars and the track together. If you can't get far enough back, try the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a wider scene. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the two cars as they pass.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Fjellveien (Fjellveien stop on the Fløibanen line, then a short walk uphill). Two funicular cars passing each other on the track, so the railway itself is the subject of the frame. Check the exact spot on the map before you set off.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the track along one of the diagonal lines so the climb is clear. Wait until the blue and red cars are level with each other, then take the photo. For a different view, Fisketorget shows the white lower station building from the harbour side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cars to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the red and blue stay rich. Switch on Live Photos or motion to catch the moment the cars pass, then choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the cars run more often and you won't wait long for them to pass. Check the Fløibanen timetable before you go.

text.access_note: The funicular is a ticketed service with ticket barriers at the stations, so check the official site before you go; Fjellveien itself is a public street.
claims_not_in_sources: Fisketorget (the fish market) is a short way from the lower station in the city centre.
Fjellveien is a public street where you can walk and photograph without a ticket.
The Fjellveien stop is on the hillside above the lower station, so the lower station lies to the west of the stand-here point.
Cars passing each other at the Fjellveien spot is a recommended photo opportunity (from a single tourism page).

name: Mount Fløyen Viewpoint
label: Fløyen Viewpoint
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7669754063: the OpenStreetMap point 'Fløyfjellet'.
notes: The classic panoramic view over Bergen, the harbour and the fjord.

text.description: Mount Fløyen (Fløyfjellet) is one of the seven mountains around the centre of Bergen, and its viewpoint offers a popular view over the Bergen Peninsula. From up here the harbour, the old town roofs, the islands and the water beyond all fit into one wide scene, which is exactly what a phone camera likes. The viewpoint sits at about 320 m above sea level, close to the top of the mountain, which reaches 400 m. Most visitors arrive on the Fløibanen funicular, which climbs from Vetrlidsallmenningen in the city centre in roughly eight minutes and opened in 1918. At the top, the viewpoint was rebuilt and extended in 2002 and is known as Fløytrappene, a broad staircase running from the funicular station towards the Fløien Folkerestaurant. The steps give you different heights to shoot from, so try a few before settling. Start with a wide frame of the whole city, then move in on a detail such as the harbour, a ship or a cluster of rooftops. Keep your phone level so the horizon and the water stay straight, and watch for people leaning on the railings, who can add a sense of scale. If you have time, the signed paths along the mountain open up other angles on the same view.
text.geographic_location: Mount Fløyen rises directly above the centre of Bergen, in Bergen Municipality, Vestland county. The viewpoint is near the top station of the Fløibanen funicular, looking out over the city and the peninsula.
text.directions_text: Start from Bergen city centre and the lower Fløibanen station at Vetrlidsallmenningen. Take the funicular up to the top, where the viewpoint is right by the station. The Fløibanen funicular is the way up, and signed hiking paths also lead up the mountain. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main view, and switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want to include more of the city and the sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as boats or rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The subject is the mountain's viewpoint right where you are standing, so you are looking out over the city from the spot the map marks.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line, depending on whether the sky or the city is more interesting. Use the railings or steps as a foreground line leading into the view. Take one wide shot and one closer telephoto shot of a detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the city to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the clouds keep their detail. Try panorama mode for a sweeping view, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Clear, dry days give the longest view. Late afternoon or early evening often gives softer light, and after dark night mode can capture the city lights, but hold the phone very steady.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is near the funicular station. Check the operator's official site before you go for current information on the Fløibanen.

name: Bergenhus Fortress
label: Bergenhus Fortress
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/487821106: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bergenhus Fortress' (380 m across).
notes: One of Norway's oldest and best-preserved fortresses at the harbour entrance.

text.description:
Bergenhus Fortress sits at the entrance of Bergen harbour and is one of the oldest and best preserved stone fortifications in Norway. Long before it was a fortress, this area, then called Holmen, was the royal seat of Bergen, and in the 13th century, until 1299, Bergen was Norway's capital. Today you can still see two medieval survivors: Haakon's Hall, built around 1260, and the tower that became the Rosenkrantz Tower in the 1560s. The fortress also carries the marks of the Second World War, when the German navy built a large concrete bunker inside its walls and the buildings were badly damaged before being restored. It is still under the command of the Royal Norwegian Navy, with around 150 military personnel stationed there, and Koengen, the open central part, is known as a concert venue.

It photographs well because old stone, open grounds and the harbour all sit close together, so one walk gives you several different pictures. Try a wide shot of the grounds first, then move closer for the hall and the tower. Look for the contrast between the pale medieval stonework and the later additions. Keep any people in the frame small for a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: Bergenhus Fortress lies at the entrance of Bergen harbour, in the centre of Bergen.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is given for this spot, so head for the entrance of Bergen harbour in the centre of Bergen. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main view of the buildings. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the open grounds and walls, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for stonework and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. This gives you a first overall view before you walk in closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the main building on one of the lines, with a strip of sky above and some open ground in front. Use ultra-wide only if you can keep the edges straight, and hold the phone level so the walls do not lean. For a second picture, move closer and fill the frame with stone texture using 2x.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone walls to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its detail and the buildings do not turn into silhouettes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to old stonework than midday sun. An overcast day also works well, as it gives even colour without harsh shadows.

text.access_note: Haakon's Hall and Rosenkrantz Tower are open for public visits, but the fortress is still under the command of the Royal Norwegian Navy, so check the official site before you go for access and visiting arrangements.

text.description:
Bergen Fish Market is a lively market scene, and it suits a phone well because so much happens at close range: colourful stalls, trays of seafood, handwritten signs and people browsing. That gives you plenty of small stories to photograph as well as one wide view.

Start with a wide frame to show the market in its setting, then move in for details. Look for repeating patterns, such as rows of produce, awnings and lines of people, because they give a photo structure. Keep the market's busy edges in the frame to show it is a working place. If people are close to you, shoot a little wider and avoid pointing the phone at faces from very near. A quick smile or a nod usually goes down well before you photograph a stallholder's goods.

The market is a place for food and shopping, so be ready to step aside for customers and trolleys. Take a few frames at different heights, one at chest level and one lower, then pick the best at home. Check the official site before you go to see when the market is trading.
text.geographic_location: Bergen Fish Market, shown on the Bergen map.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so use the map to find Bergen Fish Market. From there the market lies to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main view of the market. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the stalls are crowded and you cannot step back, and to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of food and signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line of stalls along the lower third. Take one wide shot, then step in for close frames of produce or signs. Keep the horizon level, because market buildings and awnings show a tilt quickly.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest or most colourful stall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so bright signs and white ice trays do not burn out. Use portrait mode only for close subjects, such as a single tray, and ask before photographing people.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the market is open and not too crowded, so you can see the stalls clearly. Soft daylight in the morning or late afternoon is kinder on colours than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: Open public space with market stalls; check the official site before you go for trading times and any local rules.

label: Vågen Harbour
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).

text.description: Vågen is the bay at the very heart of Bergen, and it is the city's central harbour. Bergen began on its eastern shore and spread round the southern and western sides over several centuries, so a photo of the water is also a photo of the old town's beginnings. The bay is about 1,200 metres long and opens out from the larger Byfjorden. The Nordnes peninsula lies along its southern side. On the northern shore you can see Bergenhus Fortress and Bryggen, a UNESCO World Heritage Site whose old buildings include some dating back to the 11th century. That mix of open water, a central harbour and historic buildings makes it an easy place to photograph. The water gives you a clean foreground, and the shoreline gives you a line to follow across the picture. Take a few frames in different directions: one wide for the whole bay, one tighter on the far shore, and one with a boat or the water's edge in the foreground to add depth. Keep your phone steady against your body or a railing, and check the edges of the frame for stray bags and signs before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: Vågen is the bay in the centre of Bergen, in Vestland county. It has the Nordnes peninsula on its south side and Bergenhus Fortress and Bryggen on its northern shore.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the centre of Bergen, which is the area around the Vågen bay. From there the harbour is a short walk of about 458 metres to the north-west. The phone icon on the map is about 460 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the water and the buildings along the far shore. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the bay in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details across the water, such as the old buildings on the northern shore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 460 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the shoreline on the lower or upper third line so it does not cut the picture in half. Keep the horizon level. Leave some water in the foreground and let the far shore make a band across the frame. For a different version, zoom in on one stretch of the northern shore, where Bryggen and Bergenhus Fortress lie.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far shore to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or water looks too bright. Try a panorama, moving slowly and steadily, to take in the whole width of the bay. Live Photos can catch the movement of boats and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light and calmer scenes on the waterfront. If you want a night shot, use night mode and rest your elbows on something solid to keep the phone still.

text.access_note: The bay is a central part of the city, but some harbour-side and waterfront sites may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bergen Aquarium
label: Bergen Aquarium
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6637426: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bergen Aquarium' (163 m across).
notes: A popular aquarium on the tip of Nordnes.

text.description:
Bergen Aquarium sits on the Nordnes peninsula and is one of Bergen's tourist attractions. It opened on 27 August 1960, when it was considered the largest and most modern aquarium in Northern Europe. The buildings were designed in 1952 by the architects Hans Chr. Gaaserud and Helge Simers, and a cinema was added in 1995. Inside, there are more than 300 species and over 60 tanks of fish and marine invertebrates. Outside, three ponds hold seals, penguins and other fish, and there is also a tropical section with reptiles and monkeys.

For photos, the outdoor ponds are the easiest place to start. The animals are in open daylight, so your phone can pick them out without much fuss, and the buildings give you a plain, solid backdrop. Indoors, the tanks are lit more dimly and sit behind glass, so you will get better results if you take a moment over each shot. Hold the phone close to the glass to cut down reflections, and wait for a fish or an invertebrate to drift into a clear spot before you press the shutter. Seals and penguins move quickly, so take several frames and pick the best one afterwards. Keep your fingers off the lens, because a smudge shows up badly in low light.
text.geographic_location: Bergen Aquarium is on the Nordnes peninsula in Bergen.
text.directions_text: No Bergen tram stop or station is close to the aquarium, so start from the centre of Bergen and head for the Nordnes peninsula. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the aquarium site, so there is no further walking to do. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the buildings and the layout of the outdoor area. Use the default lens (1x) for the ponds and most of the tanks. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for seals and penguins across the water, but keep it for bright outdoor light, because indoors it can look grainy.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you can photograph the buildings and the outdoor ponds without going far. For the tanks inside, stand close to the glass and square on to it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the horizon or the pond edge up with one of them so the picture sits level. For the animals, get down to their eye level where you can and leave a little space in front of the direction they are heading. At a tank, fill the frame with one animal rather than trying to take in the whole display.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the animal to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the water or sky is washing out. Indoors, switch the flash off and rest the phone against the glass or a rail to keep it steady. Try Live Photos or motion for moving animals, so you can pick the sharpest moment afterwards. Night mode can help in the dim halls, but it may blur anything that moves.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go on a bright but overcast day, or in the morning, for the outdoor ponds, when the light is soft and even. Indoor tanks look much the same at any time, so pick a quieter moment if you want clear space at the glass.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and entry rules.

label: Hanseatic Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.

notes: A preserved merchant's house showing life in the Hanseatic trading era.

text.description:
The Hanseatic Museum and Schøtstuene sits in Finnegården, one of the conserved wooden buildings on Bryggen, the old waterfront in Bergen. The museum tells the story of the Hanseatic League in the city. German merchants had set up an overseas office at Bryggen by 1360, and for about four centuries the site held their assembly halls. The present building went up after the fire of 1702, which burned most of the city centre. Inside there is a trading room with a merchant's office, sleeping places for the boys and a guestroom, and all the objects are original.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the old timber itself: uneven wooden walls, narrow gables and weathered doors that look best up close. Schøtstuene was the place where cooking was done, because fire was forbidden in the other Bryggen buildings. That is a nice detail to mention in a caption.

Stand at the phone icon on the map, which is right at the building. Take one wide shot of the frontage, then move in for details such as timber joints, windows and doorways. Wooden buildings of this age usually have strong texture, so look for close-ups that show it. Rules on photography inside may apply, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Bergen, on Bryggen, the old wooden waterfront quarter. The museum is in the building called Finnegården.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Bryggen in Bergen city centre; the museum is in Finnegården, one of the conserved wooden buildings there. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local map or journey planner for the way to Bryggen. shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your wide shot from the furthest spot you can comfortably stand, then step in for close-ups.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the wooden walls straight; tilting the phone up makes the building lean. Frame a doorway or window as a smaller picture inside the picture, and include a bit of the neighbouring Bryggen buildings to show the setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the weathered timber to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright so the wood keeps its colour. Wipe the lens before shooting.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light on the wood and fewer people in the frame. Overcast days are fine for the texture of the walls.

text.description: Rosenkrantz Tower is the tall, solid stone keep at Bergenhus Fortress, beside the entrance to Bergen harbour. It is a good subject for a phone because it is one clear shape with plain stone walls, so it stands out against the sky and the greenery of the fortress grounds. The oldest part is a medieval tower from the 1270s, built under King Magnus the Lawmender as part of the royal castle. It was altered around 1520, then enlarged and reshaped in the 1560s by Scottish stonemasons and architects. The name comes from Erik Rosenkrantz, governor of the fortress from 1560 to 1568, when the tower took its present form. The fortress itself is among the oldest and best preserved stone fortifications in Norway. Several buildings in the fortress, including Haakon's Hall, were badly damaged in World War II and later restored. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m south of the subject. That is a short, easy walk, so you can try a few angles. Start with a full-length shot from a little distance. Then move closer and look for details such as the stonework, the windows and the roofline. Haakon's Hall is also inside the fortress, so you can add it to the same walk.
text.geographic_location: Rosenkrantz Tower stands inside Bergenhus Fortress, at the entrance to Bergen harbour, in the old royal part of the city. Haakon's Hall is in the same fortress.
text.directions_text: Make your way from the centre of Bergen to the harbour entrance, where Bergenhus Fortress stands. Once you are inside the fortress grounds, the tower is easy to spot. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straightforward view of the tower. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the whole height will not fit. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details of the stonework and the roofline.

name: St Mary's Church
label: St Mary's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dreggsallmenningen' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Dreggsallmenningen nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q571683: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Bergen's oldest surviving building, a 12th-century Romanesque church behind Bryggen.

text.description:
St Mary's Church (Mariakirken) is a large grey stone church with two towers, standing in the Bryggen area of central Bergen. It is the oldest surviving building in the city. Building probably began in the 1130s or 1140s and finished around 1180. It is mainly Romanesque, built largely of soapstone, and the twin towers give it a strong, simple outline that fits easily into a phone frame. In 1408 the city's large German population took the church over, and it was popularly called the German church.

Looking back toward the church, you get the facade and both towers, with the Snorre monument and the Bryggens Museum building in the same frame. The monument works well as a foreground subject, so you get a bit of context as well as the church itself.

If you have time for a second angle, try Øvregaten, the old street behind Bryggen, for a straight-on view of the south wall and facade. Nye Sandviksveien gives a side-on view of the tower and roofline, but it is worth checking on the ground. Photography is not allowed inside the church, so these are exterior shots only.
text.geographic_location: St Mary's Church is in the Bryggen area in the central part of Bergen, with an address on Dreggsallmenningen. The Bryggens Museum building and the Snorre monument are close by.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Bryggen area, which is the nearest well-known place. From Bryggen, walk to the Bryggen end of Dreggsallmenningen. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the facade, both towers and the Snorre monument together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street feels too narrow to fit everything in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Dreggsallmenningen (looking back toward the church from the Bryggen end of the street). The church's facade and twin towers, with the Snorre monument and the Bryggens Museum building alongside in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep your phone upright, so the towers do not lean. Put the Snorre monument low in the frame as a foreground subject, with the church rising behind it. For a different angle, try Øvregaten for the south wall and facade straight on.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the grey stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the towers do not wash out. With the ultra-wide, keep the church away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or on an overcast day should give even light on the grey stone and fewer people in front of the monument.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the street, but the church is a place of worship that is closed to sightseeing at weekends outside services, and photography is not allowed inside, so check the official site before you go.

label: Bergen Cathedral

text.description: Bergen Cathedral is the cathedral of the Diocese of Bjørgvin and the seat of its bishop. It is dedicated to Saint Olaf, and the first written mention of a church on this site dates from 1181. It has burned and been rebuilt several times. After the fires of 1623 and 1640 it took on the look you see today, including the square tower at the west end. That tower is the best reason to photograph it: it gives a straight-on exterior shot with a clear, simple shape. Stand on Domkirkeplassen in front of the west façade, and the façade and tower fit in one frame. For something different, look for the cannonball from the 1665 Battle of Vågen, still embedded in the exterior wall. It makes a good close-up, with the story as your caption. A third option is Lille Øvregaten, where the clock tower and steeple rise above the cobbles and the wooden houses. The church is still in use for services and concerts, so people may be coming and going at the door. Keep the doorway clear while you shoot, and check opening and service times before you plan a visit inside.
text.geographic_location: Bergen Cathedral stands on Domkirkeplassen, the square named after it, in the city of Bergen. Lille Øvregaten is another viewpoint, good for the clock tower and steeple.
text.directions_text: Walk to Domkirkeplassen, the square in front of the cathedral's west façade, and aim for the church tower. Once you are the cathedral lies to the east, about 1 minute on foot to the middle of the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the façade and tower, as it keeps the building looking natural. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is crowded or you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower top and the cannonball detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Domkirkeplassen (in front of the west façade). The cathedral's main façade and square tower, framed from the cathedral square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and hold the phone upright and level, so the tower stays straight rather than leaning. Put the tower on one of the vertical grid lines and leave a little sky above it. Ultra-wide close to the wall will make the tower lean, so step back and use 1x where you can. For a second shot, walk to Lille Øvregaten and frame the clock tower and steeple above the cobbled street and wooden houses. Up close, use zoom on the 1665 cannonball hole in the stone wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the façade doesn't turn dark. Don't use portrait mode on the building. Save it for people in front of it, and keep them away from the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime is best for a clear exterior shot. Even cloud works well, as it avoids hard shadows on the stone. Early or late in the day, there are usually fewer people in the square.

text.access_note: The cathedral is an active church with limited opening hours, so check the official site for visiting times and service times before you go; the square outside is open public space.

text.description:
Grieg Hall (Grieghallen) is a 1,500-seat concert hall in Bergen, on the square called Edvard Griegs plass. It is named after Edvard Grieg, the Bergen-born composer who was music director of the Bergen Philharmonic Orchestra from 1880 to 1882, and the orchestra still calls it home. The Danish architect Knud Munk designed it in a modernist style. Building began in 1967 and was finished by May 1978. The hall also hosted the Eurovision Song Contest in 1986.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the building's size and its strong, plain modern shape. It is a very wide building, around 184 m across, so the challenge is fitting it in without it looking small. If you walk closer, you can pick out details such as repeating lines, corners and reflections instead.

Take a few frames at different distances: one wide shot to show the whole hall, then a tighter one of a section of the facade. Keep the gridlines on to stop the horizontal lines from sloping. Check for people or parked vehicles at the edges of the frame before you press the shutter. If you want to see inside or catch a performance, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Grieg Hall stands on Edvard Griegs plass in Bergen, Norway.
text.directions_text: No Bergen tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so head for Edvard Griegs plass in Bergen. From there it is about 2 minutes on foot to reach the building itself. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the very wide building in. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. This gives you room to include a lot of the frontage.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the roof and base of the building with the horizontal lines so it looks straight. Hold the phone level and keep it at chest height. For a second shot, move closer and use telephoto to frame a section of the facade as a pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight in the morning or late afternoon usually suits large buildings best. On a bright day, check the glare. After dark, try night mode if the building is lit, and rest your phone against something steady.

text.access_note: The square and the outside of the building can be photographed from public space, but check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or attend an event.

The square is an open space about 218 m across, so it is a place for wide, scene-setting photos of everyday city life rather than a single tight shot. The best-known feature in it is the Sjømannsmonumentet, which gives your pictures a clear focal point and some height against the open space around it. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north-west of the subject. From there the monument is only about 20 m away to the south-east, so you can take in the square and the monument together without walking far. Start with a wide shot to show the scale of the square, then step in and take a second picture that fills the frame with the monument. Turn the phone upright for the monument and sideways for the square. If people are walking through, wait a moment for a gap or include them on purpose: a few figures help show how big the place is. Switch on the gridlines so the buildings at the edges stay straight, and check the corners before you press the shutter.

text.directions_text: Head for Bergen and ask for Torgallmenningen, the main square. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The Sjømannsmonumentet is about 20 m south-east of it. shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full width of the square, then switch to the default lens (1x) for the monument. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details and for pulling the monument closer without walking up to it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the monument to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its detail and the monument does not turn into a silhouette. Try a panorama only if the square is quiet, because moving people can look odd in one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: If you can, choose a time when fewer people are around. Soft daylight is kinder to the monument than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: Torgallmenningen is a public city square; check local information before you go.

text.description: Nordnes is the long finger of land that pushes out into the water right beside Bergen's city centre. Vågen, Byfjorden and Puddefjorden surround it, and the Bergen Aquarium sits at its tip. Fredriksberg Fortress, the Norwegian Institute of Marine Research and the parish church, Nykirken, are all on the peninsula too. For the classic view you don't stand on Nordnes at all. You go up to Fløyen, the summit viewpoint above the city. Guides call this the postcard view of Bergen. From the terrace the peninsula runs diagonally across the right side of a wide panorama, with Lille Lungegårdsvannet on the left and the fjord stretching away behind. Seen from above, the shape of the peninsula is easy to read, and the harbour and the mountain backdrop help fill the frame. Two guides recommend sunrise and late afternoon. If you would rather see the peninsula from the inside, Nordnesparken at the end looks out over the harbour approach and Vågen, with ships and islands framed by trees and rocks. Klosteret, in the old quarter, has a row of pastel-painted wooden houses along a narrow, pedestrian-friendly street. Start with the wide view from Fløyen, then zoom in on the peninsula for a second, tighter picture.
text.geographic_location: Nordnes is a peninsula and neighbourhood in the centre of Bergen, with the Bergen Aquarium at its tip. Fløyen, the summit above the city, is not on the peninsula itself.
text.directions_text: Start from Bergen city centre and head for Fløyen, which you can reach by the funicular or by a hiking route to the summit. In practice you see the peninsula from above rather than walking to it. Check the official site before you go for how the funicular is running. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) or the default lens (1x) to take in the whole city panorama. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the peninsula on its own.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Fløyen (summit viewpoint, looking down over the peninsula toward the fjord). The Nordnes peninsula runs diagonally across the right side of a wide city panorama, with Lille Lungegårdsvannet on the left and the fjord beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the fjord horizon on a lower line, so the city and the peninsula fill the picture. Let the peninsula run from the middle of the frame towards the right-hand edge. Try panorama mode to capture the whole sweep from the harbour to the mountains. For a different view, Nordnesparken at the tip looks out over Vågen, with ships and islands framed by trees and rocks.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the peninsula to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Take one wide shot and one zoomed shot from the same spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise and late afternoon, according to two guides.

text.access_note: Fløyen is reached by a paid funicular (a hiking route also reaches the summit), so check the official site before you go; Nordnesparken is reached on foot, and the path can be steep.

label: Lille Lungegårdsvann
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).

notes: The city-centre lake with its fountain and promenade.

text.description:
Lille Lungegårdsvannet, also known as Smålungeren, is a small lake in a park right in the centre of Bergen. It is about 5 acres in size and has an unusual octagonal shape, which gives it a neat, geometric look that suits a phone photo. A large decorative fountain stands in the middle of the water, so you have an obvious focal point with open sky and reflections around it.

The lake used to be much larger. As the city grew, the edges were filled in to make new land, and the sides were straightened until the octagon reached its present shape in the mid-20th century. It was once joined to the bay of Store Lungegårdsvannet by a short strait. That strait was filled in in 1926 and replaced by an underground culvert. Because the two waters are still connected underground, the level of the lake rises and falls a little with the tide.

For photos, look for the fountain with the park paths and trees around it, or use the straight edges of the lake as leading lines. On a calm day the water can mirror the sky and the buildings. The lake is 279 m across, so there is room to step back and try a wide view as well as a closer shot of the fountain. Check the water and the fountain as you arrive, because their appearance changes with the weather and the wind.
text.geographic_location: The lake lies in a park in the centre of Bergen, in Vestland county, close to the Store Lungegårdsvannet bay.
text.directions_text: Head for the park in the centre of Bergen. From there the lake is about 2 minutes on foot to the north-east. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lake and fountain together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more of the octagon and the park around it. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the fountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the fountain on one of the crossing points, rather than dead centre, to leave room for sky or reflections. Keep the shoreline edge straight along a gridline so the octagon looks tidy. Then take a second shot from a lower position, close to the water, for stronger reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the water spray does not turn white. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the fountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or a still, overcast day usually gives the calmest water and the best reflections. Late afternoon can give softer light across the park.

text.access_note: The lake is in a city-centre park, but check the official site before you go for any local restrictions or work in the park.

notes: A 13th-century stone royal banquet hall inside Bergenhus.

text.description:
Haakon's Hall (Håkonshallen) is a medieval stone feast hall inside Bergenhus Fortress, at the entrance to Bergen harbour. It was built in the middle of the 13th century in the reign of King Håkon Håkonsson, and it is the largest secular medieval building in Norway. It is built in the Gothic style, and the plain stone walls and steep lines suit a phone photo taken from a little way back. The Rosenkrantz Tower is in the same fortress.

The hall has had a rough history. It was hit by fire as early as 1266, and was burnt in 1429 by the Victual Brothers. Later it was used as a storage building, and in 1840 it was proved to be King Håkon's old feast hall. It was restored in the 1890s, then badly damaged by fire on 20 April 1944. After a second restoration it reopened on 11 September 1961, exactly 700 years after its first recorded use. The hall is now used for occasional concerts and official banquets.

For photographs, the open lawns and paths of the fortress let you step back and fit the whole building in. Take one wide shot to show the setting and one closer shot for the stonework and the roofline. Keep your phone upright so the walls stay straight.
text.geographic_location: Haakon's Hall stands inside Bergenhus Fortress, at the entrance to Bergen harbour in Bergen, Norway. The Rosenkrantz Tower is in the same fortress.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so plan to reach the fortress on foot. Walk towards the middle of the fortress and look for the hall. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole hall. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the walls and cannot step back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the stonework, windows and roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Face north-east, towards the middle of the fortress, and walk into the grounds until you can see the hall and fit it in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the hall's vertical edges up with them so the walls stay straight. Keep the phone upright and level for the full building. Include a bit of lawn or path in the foreground for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building stays dark enough to show detail rather than going pale. Wipe your lens first, as a smudge shows up as haze on a pale sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone and fewer people in the grounds. On an overcast day the walls photograph evenly and you can shoot at any time.

text.access_note: The hall and the Rosenkrantz Tower are open for public visits, but entry rules and times can change, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Permanenten is a museum building in Bergen that is part of the KODE art museums. It is a good subject for a phone photo because it is a formal, Renaissance Revival-style façade, with the kind of symmetry and detail that rewards a careful frame. The museum began in 1887 as an idea of Johan Bøgh. In 1896 it moved into a permanent exhibition building designed by Henry Bucher. The building caught fire during the 1916 Bergen Fire but was saved. Inside, the collections focus on crafts from the past 500 years, including silver, furniture, glass, porcelain and textiles. There is also a well-known Chinese collection. Depending on where you end up, you may have to choose between a tight shot of the façade and a wider shot that shows its surroundings. Try both. Turn on the gridlines in your camera app to keep the vertical lines of the walls straight. Hold the phone level, because tilting it makes the building lean. If you can't fit the whole building in, step back, or switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) and keep the phone upright. Details such as windows, stonework and the entrance also make good close-ups with the telephoto lens (2x or more).

KODE is Bergen's group of art museums, and the subject here is the museum buildings in the city centre. The phone icon on the map is about 290 m north-west of the subject. That makes it a good spot for a simple, tidy photo to remember the visit by, especially if you plan to go inside afterwards.

It might be the museum frontage with some sky above it, or a wider street scene with people walking through. Turn on the gridlines and line up the building with one of the vertical lines so it doesn't look as if it is leaning. Wait for a gap if people walk through the frame, or let them stay in the picture to give a sense of scale.

Bergen's weather changes quickly, so check the sky before you set up. Overcast light is kind to building fronts, and wet pavements can add a pleasant reflection. If you want pictures inside the galleries, rules on photography can differ from room to room, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: Keep the map open and head for the museum. The phone icon on the map is about 290 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the museum closer without walking towards it. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is useful only if you step in close and want to fit in the whole frontage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 290 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the building on a vertical line to keep the edges straight. Leave a little foreground, such as the pavement or some trees, to give depth. Take one wide shot and one zoomed shot so you have both the setting and the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright and washing out. Hold the phone with both hands and keep your elbows tucked in for sharper zoomed shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight on an overcast day or in the morning gives even colours on the building. In the evening, use night mode if the light fades, and hold still for the full exposure.

text.access_note: Check the official KODE website for visiting information before you go.
